questions.stem: A 28-year-old physiologist studies the body distribution of magnesium. Approximately what fraction of total body magnesium is located in the extracellular fluid?
explanations: Correct. Only ~1% of total body Mg2+ is in the ECF; serum levels poorly reflect total body stores. ~50% is in bone (largely non-exchangeable), ~49% is intracellular (muscle, liver, soft tissue), and ~1% is in ECF. Patients can have profound intracellular depletion with normal-appearing serum Mg.
Incorrect. 10% is too high.
Incorrect. 30% does not match any compartment.
Incorrect. ~50% is in BONE, not ECF.
Incorrect. 99% is in bone + intracellular combined.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old researcher studies renal Mg2+ handling. Which nephron segment reabsorbs the LARGEST fraction of filtered magnesium?
explanations: Incorrect. PCT reabsorbs only ~15–25% of filtered Mg2+.

Correct. The TAL reabsorbs ~60–70% of filtered Mg2+ paracellularly through claudin-16/19 tight junctions, driven by the lumen-positive transepithelial voltage from ROMK-mediated K+ recycling. Loop diuretics abolish this and produce Mg2+ wasting.
Incorrect. DCT reabsorbs only ~5–10% (active, via TRPM6).
Incorrect. Collecting duct does not principally handle Mg2+.
Incorrect. Same.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old physiologist studies Mg2+ uptake in the DCT. Which apical channel mediates fine-tuned active Mg2+ reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule?
explanations: Incorrect. TRPV5 is the apical Ca2+ channel in the DCT.

Correct. TRPM6 is the apical Mg2+ channel in DCT cells. Loss-of-function mutations cause autosomal recessive familial hypomagnesemia with secondary hypocalcemia. TRPM6 is also downregulated in chronic thiazide use, contributing to thiazide-induced hypomagnesemia.
Incorrect. ROMK is the apical K+ channel.
Incorrect. NCC is the Na+-Cl− cotransporter (thiazide target).
Incorrect. ENaC is the K+-sparing diuretic target.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with chronic alcoholism and chronic diarrhea has serum Mg 1.2 mg/dL. He has tremor, tetany, and hyperreflexia. Which best characterizes severe hypomagnesemia?
explanations: Correct. Severe hypomagnesemia (Mg <1.0–1.2 mg/dL) presents with neuromuscular hyperexcitability — tetany, tremor, weakness, hyperreflexia, seizures — and increased risk of cardiac arrhythmias including torsades de pointes (especially with concurrent hypokalemia or QT-prolonging drugs).
Incorrect. Those values describe HYPERmagnesemia.
Incorrect. Severe hypermagnesemia.
Incorrect. Lab artifacts are not the main concern here.
Incorrect. The clinical situation is dangerous.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman on chronic furosemide has Mg 1.4, K+ 2.8 (refractory to KCl supplementation). Which mechanism explains why magnesium repletion is critical for correcting her potassium?
choices: Low intracellular Mg2+ removes ROMK inhibition
Mg2+ binds K+ in the gut
explanations: Incorrect. Mg2+ does not principally activate ROMK; it inhibits it.

Correct. Intracellular Mg2+ normally INHIBITS ROMK (the apical K+ channel in collecting duct principal cells). When intracellular Mg2+ is low, this inhibition is removed and ROMK conducts more K+ into the lumen — perpetuating renal K+ wasting. This is why concurrent hypomagnesemia produces refractory hypokalemia, and why Mg2+ repletion is essential before K+ replacement will work.
Incorrect. Mg2+ does not principally bind K+.
Incorrect. Mg2+ does not principally affect aldosterone.
Incorrect. Mg2+ does not principally regulate Na+/K+-ATPase.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with severe Crohn disease and short bowel syndrome has Mg 1.0 mg/dL. Which mechanism best explains her hypomagnesemia?
explanations: Incorrect. Renal wasting is plausible if she had diuretics, but the Crohn / short-bowel context points to GI loss.

Correct. GI causes are common: chronic diarrhea, short bowel syndrome, malabsorption (Crohn, celiac), pancreatic insufficiency, and PPI-related Mg wasting (long-term PPI reduces TRPM6 expression in intestine). Mg2+ absorption is principally in the small intestine via passive paracellular flow plus active TRPM6.
Incorrect. Adrenal insufficiency does not principally cause hypomagnesemia.
Incorrect. No diuretic exposure described.
Incorrect. The hypomagnesemia is real.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man on long-term omeprazole for GERD has Mg 1.3 mg/dL. Which best explains the proton-pump inhibitor effect?
choices: PPI reduces intestinal TRPM6-mediated Mg2+ absorption
explanations: Incorrect. PPIs do not principally cause renal wasting.

Correct. Long-term PPI use is associated with hypomagnesemia, likely via reduced TRPM6-mediated active intestinal Mg2+ absorption (the mechanism is incompletely understood but TRPM6 expression and function are reduced). FDA warning issued in 2011. Resolves on discontinuation. More common with high-dose, prolonged use, and concurrent diuretic therapy. Other PPI long-term concerns: B12 deficiency, Clostridium difficile, fractures, AKI/AIN.
Incorrect. PPIs do not chemically chelate Mg2+.
Incorrect. Sweat is not the principal mechanism.
Incorrect. PPI-related hypomagnesemia is a recognized association.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman with metastatic colon cancer is receiving cetuximab. She develops Mg 1.1 mg/dL and weakness. Which mechanism best explains cetuximab-induced hypomagnesemia?
choices: EGFR antagonism impairs renal TRPM6 function
Cetuximab causes GI bleeding losing Mg2+
explanations: Incorrect. Cetuximab is a monoclonal antibody, not a diuretic.

Correct. EGFR inhibitors (cetuximab, panitumumab) cause hypomagnesemia via inhibition of EGFR signaling that normally activates TRPM6 in the DCT. Loss of EGFR-driven TRPM6 activation produces renal Mg2+ wasting. Hypomagnesemia is dose- and duration-dependent and very common with these agents (~50% of patients on cetuximab develop low Mg). Aggressive Mg2+ replacement is often needed.
Incorrect. Cetuximab does not principally cause GI bleeding.
Incorrect. Calcimimetics affect calcium, not magnesium.
Incorrect. Tumor cells do not consume plasma Mg2+.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man being treated for an aggressive infection with high-dose IV gentamicin develops Mg 1.0 and hypokalemia after 1 week of therapy. Which mechanism best explains aminoglycoside-induced hypomagnesemia?
choices: Aminoglycosides cause renal tubular Mg2+ wasting
Aminoglycosides cause cellular shift of Mg2+
explanations: Incorrect. The mechanism is renal, not GI.

Correct. Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) cause proximal tubular injury and TAL/DCT dysfunction, producing renal Mg2+ (and Ca2+, K+) wasting. Onset typically within 1–2 weeks. Other nephrotoxins with similar effects: cisplatin, amphotericin B, foscarnet, calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine, tacrolimus). Monitor electrolytes routinely; replete Mg2+ aggressively.
Incorrect. Aminoglycosides do not inhibit ENaC.
Incorrect. The mechanism is renal, not cellular shift.
Incorrect. Aminoglycosides do not chelate Mg2+.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with chronic alcoholism has Mg 1.1 mg/dL and Ca 7.6 mg/dL with inappropriately LOW PTH. Which best explains the hypocalcemia?
explanations: Correct. Severe hypomagnesemia (typically Mg <1.0–1.5) IMPAIRS PTH secretion AND parathyroid end-organ responsiveness, producing functional hypoparathyroidism with hypocalcemia. The hypocalcemia is REFRACTORY to calcium replacement until Mg2+ is repleted. Always check Mg2+ in any unexplained hypocalcemia, especially in alcoholics, malnutrition, chronic diuretic use, or PPI use.
Incorrect. Pancreatitis can cause hypocalcemia (saponification) but does not lower PTH.
Incorrect. Vit D toxicity raises Ca2+.
Incorrect. Primary hyperparathyroidism has elevated PTH.
Incorrect. The hypocalcemia is real.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman with chronic fatigue has Mg 1.4 mg/dL, K+ 3.0, HCO3− 32, hypocalciuria, and normal blood pressure. She has elevated renin and aldosterone. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanations: Incorrect. Bartter has HYPERcalciuria.

Correct. Gitelman syndrome — autosomal recessive loss-of-function in NCC. Phenocopies chronic thiazide use: hypokalemic alkalosis, HYPOmagnesemia (DCT atrophy reduces TRPM6 activity), HYPOcalciuria (the distinguishing feature from Bartter), normal-low BP, elevated renin/aldosterone. Treatment: K+ and Mg2+ supplementation, NaCl, sometimes K+-sparing diuretic.
Incorrect. Liddle has hypertension.
Incorrect. Conn has hypertension.
Incorrect. Type 1 RTA features acidosis and hypokalemia.

questions.stem: A child has hypomagnesemia, hypercalciuria, nephrocalcinosis, and progressive CKD from infancy. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in claudin-16. Which best characterizes this disorder?
explanations: Correct. FHHNC — autosomal recessive loss-of-function mutations in CLDN16 or CLDN19 (claudins of the TAL paracellular pathway). The TAL cannot properly reabsorb Mg2+ or Ca2+ paracellularly. Result: hypomagnesemia, HYPERcalciuria with nephrocalcinosis and renal stones, progressive CKD often presenting in childhood. Treatment: thiazides reduce hypercalciuria; aggressive Mg2+ replacement; eventually transplant if ESRD.
Incorrect. Bartter has hypokalemic alkalosis dominating, often with hypomagnesemia, but classically without nephrocalcinosis as the principal feature.
Incorrect. Gitelman has HYPOcalciuria.
Incorrect. Liddle has hypertension.
Incorrect. FHH is benign and features hypocalciuria with hypercalcemia.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with severe hypomagnesemia (Mg 0.9) has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. ECG shows a wide QRS complex and prolonged QT. Which therapy is most appropriate?
explanations: Incorrect. Oral Mg is for non-urgent replacement; this patient needs IV.

Correct. Severe symptomatic hypomagnesemia (seizure, tetany, arrhythmia) is treated with IV magnesium sulfate — typically 1–2 g over 15–60 min, followed by continuous infusion or repeat dosing. Concurrent IV calcium and K+ replacement may be needed. Monitor DTRs and ECG; reduced reflexes are a sign of overdose.
Incorrect. Calcium is not the primary treatment for Mg deficiency itself; it is given separately if hypocalcemia is symptomatic.
Incorrect. Thiazides actually cause Mg2+ wasting.
Incorrect. Vit D does not directly correct Mg deficiency.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman with severe preeclampsia receives IV magnesium sulfate. Six hours later she has loss of deep tendon reflexes, blood pressure 90/60, and Mg level 9 mg/dL. Which is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
explanations: Incorrect. More Mg worsens toxicity.

Correct. Hypermagnesemia toxicity progresses: loss of DTRs (Mg ~5–7) → respiratory depression (~7–10) → cardiac arrest (>12). Treatment: STOP Mg; IV calcium gluconate ANTAGONIZES Mg2+ at the neuromuscular junction (similar physiology to calcium's role in hyperkalemia membrane stabilization); supportive care; furosemide if euvolemic to enhance excretion; dialysis for severe / refractory.
Incorrect. Furosemide alone is not the immediate first step (though useful adjunct).
Incorrect. Insulin/glucose is for hyperkalemia.
Incorrect. Dialysis is reserved for severe / refractory cases.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with end-stage renal disease takes a magnesium-containing antacid for indigestion. Two weeks later she has Mg 7.5, weakness, and reduced reflexes. Which best explains the hypermagnesemia?
explanations: Correct. Hypermagnesemia is rare with normal renal function (kidneys readily excrete excess Mg2+). In ESRD or AKI, excretion is impaired and exogenous Mg2+ from antacids (Mg(OH)2, milk of magnesia), laxatives, or supplements can accumulate. Other causes: IV Mg in eclampsia treatment, lithium therapy, adrenal insufficiency, tumor lysis. Educate ESRD patients to avoid Mg-containing OTC products.
Incorrect. Pancreatitis is associated with HYPOcalcemia, not principally hypermagnesemia.
Incorrect. Hemolysis releases K+ more than Mg2+.
Incorrect. The hypermagnesemia is real.
Incorrect. Adrenal insufficiency is a cause but the antacid history is more direct here.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man on chronic loop diuretic for HFrEF has Mg 1.4. Which mechanism best explains loop diuretic-induced hypomagnesemia?
explanations: Incorrect. The mechanism is renal, not GI.

Correct. Loop diuretics inhibit NKCC2 in the TAL, abolishing the K+ recycling and lumen-positive voltage that drives PARACELLULAR Mg2+ (and Ca2+) reabsorption through claudin-16/19. Result: renal Mg2+ wasting. Same mechanism produces hypercalciuria.
Incorrect. TRPM6 is in the DCT; loop diuretics do not principally inhibit it.
Incorrect. Increased aldosterone affects K+ secretion, not principally Mg2+.
Incorrect. Loop diuretics do not directly injure the adrenal cortex.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman on chronic thiazide develops Mg 1.5 mg/dL. Which mechanism best explains thiazide-induced hypomagnesemia?
choices: DCT atrophy with reduced TRPM6 expression
explanations: Incorrect. Thiazides act in the DCT, not principally TAL.

Correct. Chronic thiazide therapy causes structural and functional atrophy of DCT cells with downregulation of TRPM6 expression — reducing apical Mg2+ uptake. Combined with the proximal volume contraction effect, the net result is Mg2+ wasting. Hypomagnesemia from chronic thiazide is common and contributes to refractory hypokalemia by removing Mg2+-dependent ROMK inhibition.
Incorrect. Thiazides do not chelate Mg2+ in the gut.
Incorrect. Aldosterone elevation does not directly cause Mg2+ wasting.
Incorrect. Hypomagnesemia is real.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with chronic chemotherapy receives high-dose cisplatin. Within 2 weeks she has Mg 1.1 and K+ 3.0. Which best explains the cisplatin effect?
explanations: Correct. Cisplatin is a recognized nephrotoxin causing both proximal and distal tubular injury. The DCT effect downregulates TRPM6 and reduces Mg2+ reabsorption, often producing severe and persistent hypomagnesemia (sometimes lasting months after therapy). Concurrent K+ and Ca2+ wasting is common. Aggressive electrolyte replacement and adequate hydration during cisplatin therapy reduce nephrotoxicity.
Incorrect. Cisplatin is not a calcimimetic.
Incorrect. Cisplatin does not principally cause adrenal insufficiency.
Incorrect. Cisplatin does not principally cause hemolysis.
Incorrect. The hypomagnesemia is real.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man on chronic tacrolimus after a renal transplant develops Mg 1.5. Which mechanism best explains calcineurin inhibitor-induced hypomagnesemia?
explanations: Incorrect. The mechanism is renal.

Correct. Calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, cyclosporine) downregulate TRPM6 expression in the DCT, producing renal Mg2+ wasting. Hypomagnesemia is common in transplant recipients on these agents and contributes to seizure risk (especially with neurologic toxicity already a concern with tacrolimus). Aggressive oral or IV repletion; sometimes amiloride is added (it has Mg2+-sparing effect).
Incorrect. Tacrolimus does not chelate Mg2+ in the gut.
Incorrect. Tacrolimus does not principally cause pancreatitis.
Incorrect. Tacrolimus does not principally cause hemolysis.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman has refractory hypomagnesemia despite adequate oral Mg replacement. Adding which K+-sparing diuretic can paradoxically reduce her renal Mg2+ wasting?
explanations: Incorrect. Loop diuretics WORSEN Mg2+ wasting.
Incorrect. Thiazides also worsen Mg2+ wasting.

Correct. Amiloride blocks ENaC in the cortical collecting duct, with secondary effect of REDUCING distal Mg2+ wasting (the mechanism involves modulating the lumen-negative voltage that influences Mg2+ secretion in the late nephron). Used as adjunctive therapy in refractory renal Mg2+ wasting (e.g., from cisplatin, calcineurin inhibitors, Gitelman). Risk: hyperkalemia.
Incorrect. Acetazolamide is not Mg2+-sparing.
Incorrect. Mannitol is osmotic; not Mg2+-sparing.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man has Mg 1.4, K+ 3.0, and recurrent ventricular arrhythmias. After Mg2+ supplementation, his arrhythmias resolve. Which arrhythmia is most classically associated with hypomagnesemia?
explanations: Incorrect. Atrial flutter is not the classic Mg2+ arrhythmia.
Incorrect. Bradycardia is not the classic association.

Correct. Torsades de pointes — polymorphic ventricular tachycardia in the setting of QT prolongation — is the classic arrhythmia associated with hypomagnesemia (often combined with hypokalemia and QT-prolonging drugs). IV Mg2+ is first-line treatment regardless of measured Mg level. Other Mg2+-related arrhythmias: atrial fibrillation, ventricular ectopy, polymorphic VT.
Incorrect. AV block is not the classic association.
Incorrect. RBBB is not the classic association.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman with eclampsia is given IV magnesium sulfate as seizure prophylaxis. Which best explains MgSO4's role in eclampsia?
explanations: Incorrect. MgSO4 has modest antihypertensive effect but is not principally a BP-lowering agent.

Correct. IV MgSO4 is first-line for prevention and treatment of eclamptic seizures. Mechanisms include NMDA-receptor blockade (anticonvulsant), cerebral vasodilation (counters cerebral vasospasm), and stabilization of the neuromuscular junction. Standard regimen: 4–6 g IV loading + 1–2 g/h infusion. Monitor: DTRs (loss = early toxicity), respiratory rate, urine output, Mg level. Antidote for toxicity: IV calcium gluconate.
Incorrect. MgSO4 is not principally diuretic.
Incorrect. Not a corticosteroid.
Incorrect. While Mg has tocolytic effects, the principal eclampsia indication is seizure prevention/treatment.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man has Mg 0.9 mg/dL after recovery from severe DKA with insulin therapy. Which mechanism best explains the post-DKA hypomagnesemia?
explanations: Correct. DKA produces total-body Mg2+ depletion through osmotic diuresis (renal Mg2+ losses) before treatment. After insulin therapy, the cellular shift effect (insulin drives Mg2+ INTO cells along with K+ and phosphate) unmasks the depletion as serum Mg2+ falls. Replete Mg2+ alongside K+ and phosphate during DKA correction.
Incorrect. DKA is not principally complicated by pancreatitis.
Incorrect. GI loss is not the principal route in DKA.
Incorrect. Aldosterone is not the principal driver.
Incorrect. Ketones do not directly damage TRPM6.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old patient is being given IV magnesium for severe hypomagnesemia. The clinician wants to monitor for toxicity. Which clinical finding is the EARLIEST sign of hypermagnesemia?
explanations: Incorrect. Cardiac arrest is the latest, terminal sign.

Correct. Loss of deep tendon reflexes is the EARLIEST clinical sign of hypermagnesemia (Mg ~5–7 mg/dL). Progression: → flaccid paralysis → respiratory depression (~7–10) → bradycardia, hypotension → cardiac arrest (>12). Routine monitoring of DTRs, respiratory rate, and BP allows early detection. Treatment: stop Mg, IV calcium, supportive care.
Incorrect. Coma is a later finding.
Incorrect. Respiratory paralysis is later.
Incorrect. Asystole is terminal.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man has Mg 1.5 mg/dL discovered on routine labs. He is asymptomatic with no medication use that explains it. Which is the most appropriate next step?
explanations: Incorrect. IV is reserved for severe / symptomatic.

Correct. Mild asymptomatic hypomagnesemia is treated with oral magnesium salts (Mg oxide, gluconate, citrate); a 24-hour urinary Mg measurement helps distinguish renal wasting (urine Mg >24 mg/day in setting of low serum Mg suggests renal loss) from extra-renal causes (urine Mg <24 mg/day suggests GI loss or redistribution). Identify and address the underlying cause; oral supplementation may be needed long-term in chronic GI or renal causes.
Incorrect. Dialysis is for hypermagnesemia, not hypomagnesemia.
Incorrect. Hypomagnesemia warrants attention even if asymptomatic.
Incorrect. Furosemide worsens Mg2+ wasting.
